findings.title: close()/terminate() permanently destroy the shared queue pool, breaking processing after any rebalance
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() (and terminate()) calls self.queue_pool.shutdown(), which stops all OrderedQueueWorker threads and shuts down every internal queue.Queue permanently. The FixedQueuePool instance, however, is created once in ResultsStrategyFactory.__init__ and reused across every subsequent call to create_with_partitions (e.g. after Kafka partition rebalances) — exactly like parallel_executor/multiprocessing_pool in result_consumer.py, which are intentionally only torn down in ResultsStrategyFactory.shutdown() at final process exit, never per-strategy-close. Because arroyo calls close()/terminate() on the current strategy whenever it is being replaced (which happens on every rebalance, not just final shutdown), the first rebalance kills the workers and shuts down the queues. Any create_with_partitions call afterwards reuses the now-dead queue_pool: submit() pushes items into shut-down queues (raising queue.ShutDown, silently caught and the offset marked 'complete' without any real processing), so messages after the first rebalance are effectively dropped while the consumer appears healthy.

findings.title: Uses Python 3.13-only queue.Queue.shutdown()/queue.ShutDown API
findings.body: FixedQueuePool.shutdown() calls q.shutdown(immediate=False), and OrderedQueueWorker.run() catches queue.ShutDown. Both queue.Queue.shutdown() and the queue.ShutDown exception were introduced in Python 3.13. On earlier Python runtimes, q.shutdown() raises AttributeError; since that call is wrapped in a bare 'except Exception', the failure is silently logged rather than propagated, meaning the queue is never actually put into a shutdown state. Worker threads blocked in work_queue.get() are consequently never woken and will hang indefinitely instead of shutting down, defeating the entire purpose of FixedQueuePool.shutdown()/close().

findings.title: Offsets are marked complete (and committed) even when processing raises an exception
findings.body: In OrderedQueueWorker.run(), the finally block always calls self.offset_tracker.complete_offset(...) regardless of whether result_processor succeeded or raised an exception caught by the preceding 'except Exception' clause. This contradicts the guarantee stated in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy's docstring ('Only commits offsets after successful processing'): a message whose processing failed is treated identically to a successfully processed one, so its offset becomes eligible for commit and will never be retried or reprocessed — a processing failure silently advances the committed offset past the failed message.

findings.title: test_thread_queue_parallel_error_handling asserts behavior inconsistent with the implementation
findings.body: This test mocks the result processor to raise on the first call and succeed on the second, then asserts `len(committed_offsets) == 0 or test_partition not in committed_offsets`, implying a processing failure should block the offset commit. But per OrderedQueueWorker.run()'s finally block, offsets are always marked complete regardless of exceptions, so the commit loop should still compute and commit an offset for test_partition once both items complete (which happens almost immediately since the mocked calls return synchronously). This makes the assertion likely to fail or flake against the real implementation, or indicates the test does not actually validate any failure-handling guarantee.

findings.title: Per-queue queue.Queue() has no maxsize, so the claimed backpressure doesn't exist
findings.body: Each internal queue created in FixedQueuePool.__init__ (queue.Queue()) is unbounded, and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.submit() never raises arroyo's MessageRejected to signal backpressure regardless of queue depth. Despite the docstrings on FixedQueuePool and SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy explicitly claiming 'Natural backpressure when queues fill up', no bound is enforced anywhere, so a slow or stuck group (or an overall slow downstream) can grow its queue without limit while the consumer keeps reading from Kafka, risking unbounded memory growth instead of the intended backpressure.

findings.title: get_committable_offsets iterates the offsets dict without a lock protecting its structure
findings.body: get_committable_offsets() takes list(self.all_offsets.keys()) and then separately locks per-partition to read self.all_offsets[partition]. The all_offsets defaultdict's key set can be mutated from another thread calling add_offset for a partition never seen before (defaultdict.__missing__ inserting a new key) without any lock protecting the dict's structure itself — only the per-partition lock (created lazily, after the key may already need to be inserted) guards the inner set contents. Enumerating dict.keys() into a list while another thread inserts a new key concurrently can race, and in CPython can even raise RuntimeError: dictionary changed size during iteration, which would crash the background commit loop thread.

findings.title: Offset commits are issued from a dedicated background thread instead of the main strategy thread
findings.body: _commit_loop runs on its own daemon thread started in SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.__init__ and calls self.commit_function(committable), which ultimately invokes the arroyo `commit` callback passed into create_with_partitions. Arroyo processing strategies are designed to be driven single-threadedly by the StreamProcessor's main loop (submit/poll/join); none of the other modes in this same file (serial, parallel, batched-parallel) invoke the commit callback from a separate thread. Calling `commit` concurrently with the main thread's own poll()/submit() activity deviates from that contract and risks races in whatever internal bookkeeping the Commit implementation performs, since it is not documented/guaranteed to be safe for concurrent use from worker threads.

findings.title: close() shuts down the queue pool without draining it first
findings.body: SimpleQueueProcessingStrategy.close() immediately calls self.queue_pool.shutdown() without first calling the already-implemented FixedQueuePool.wait_until_empty() helper. FixedQueuePool.shutdown() only gives each worker a 5 second join() timeout; if there is still a backlog when close() runs, items may not finish processing within that window (a timed-out join() does not stop the thread, it just stops waiting), so close() can return while unprocessed/uncommitted work is still in flight, risking those messages being left in an inconsistent processed/committed state depending on what happens after close() returns.
